props.title: Don't Look Up
props.initialSlug: The end is nigh. Don't blink.

sections.content: **Don't Look Up (2021)** (2021) stands as Adam McKay's most ambitious satirical punch at modern society's inability to face existential threats. Like his earlier **The Big Short** (2015), McKay weaponizes star power and dark humor to tackle serious issues, but here he aims bigger - using a planet-killing comet as an obvious metaphor for climate change and global catastrophes. The film follows astronomers played by Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence as they desperately try to warn a world more interested in social media, politics, and profit than impending doom. It's part of a new wave of climate anxiety films like **First Reformed** (2017) and **Snowpiercer** (2013) that channel environmental dread into narrative tension.

sections.content: The film's DNA traces back to disaster movies, but with a crucial twist - instead of heroic last-minute saves like in **Deep Impact** (1998) or **Armageddon** (1998), **Don't Look Up** suggests we might be too dysfunctional to save ourselves. This connects it to a darker strain of apocalyptic cinema like **Melancholia** (2011) and **Take Shelter** (2011), where the threat isn't just external but tied to human nature itself. McKay's signature fourth-wall breaks and info-dumps, refined in **The Big Short** (2015), here serve to highlight the absurdity of ignoring scientific consensus.

The film's star-studded cast, including Meryl Streep as a Trump-like president and Mark Rylance as a tech CEO blend of Zuckerberg/Musk/Bezos, reflects Hollywood's increasing willingness to directly challenge power structures. This follows films like **Sorry to Bother You** (2018) and **The Laundromat** (2019) in using surreal humor and direct address to make systemic criticism more palatable. The ending particularly echoes Dr. Strangelove (1964) in its dark absurdist take on human nature facing extinction. SUBHEAD: Evolution of Climate Crisis Cinema

sections.content: **Don't Look Up** represents a shift in how cinema addresses climate change - moving from the spectacular disasters of **2012** (2009) to more complex metaphorical approaches like **Mother!** (2017) and **Beasts of the Southern Wild** (2012). The film's viral marketing campaign and Netflix platform also highlight how streaming is changing how message movies reach audiences, similar to how **An Inconvenient Truth** (2006) used documentary format to spread climate awareness.
